subtopics.title: Echo and reverberation: arrival overlap and detectability
subtopics.learning_goal: Distinct echoes and reverberation depend on arrival separation, signal duration, amplitudes, detection resolution and reflection persistence, not a universal distance threshold.

science_records.claim: Distinct echoes and reverberation depend on arrival separation, signal duration, amplitudes, detection resolution and reflection persistence, not a universal distance threshold.
science_records.law_or_model: For a stated pulse model, reflected delay Δt=(L_ref−L_direct)/v; arrival interval [t,t+τ] for duration τ; separability depends on the specified detector/overlap criterion.
assumptions: Linear pulse-duration model assumes negligible distortion and known leading times; real signals can interfere or change shape.
Quiet-gap and amplitude thresholds are explicitly specified task models, not universal human criteria.
conditions_and_limits: Linear pulse-duration model assumes negligible distortion and known leading times; real signals can interfere or change shape.
Quiet-gap and amplitude thresholds are explicitly specified task models, not universal human criteria.
Use relative arrival times consistently; absolute time from emission differs from excess delay.

science_records.units_and_signs: Times s or ms, path lengths m, relative amplitude dimensionless when supplied; no universal human threshold assumed.

core1a.phenomenon: A short clap may produce a distinct repeat in one room but a long blended sound in another.
core1a.scientific_narrative:
When a source produces a short pulse in a room, part of the sound arrives directly and parts reflect from surfaces. A sufficiently delayed detectable return may be heard as a distinct echo. Numerous overlapping reflected arrivals can prolong the sound after the source stops; this persistence is reverberation. The distinction depends on the source signal, the listener or detector, the strength of returns and their timing. The familiar school estimate of a tenth of a second for a separately perceived echo is a rough contextual guideline, not an exact universal rule.

Draw a time axis beginning at emission. A direct arrival has a travel time L_direct/v; a reflected arrival has L_ref/v. The difference is the excess delay, not necessarily the full return time. A pulse of duration τ occupies an interval from its leading arrival t to t+τ if propagation does not substantially change its shape. Two finite pulses overlap if their intervals intersect; even nonoverlapping intervals may not be distinguishable if the detector needs a minimum quiet gap or a return is too weak. For a specified model with required quiet gap g, successive nonoverlapping pulses are separately resolved only when their leading times differ by at least τ+g. This is a stipulated detector rule, not a claim about all human hearing.

An example: pulses of duration 12 ms start at 0, 8 and 40 ms relative to the direct arrival. The first two overlap from 8 to12 ms and together occupy 0–20 ms; the third begins 20 ms after that cluster ends. If all are detectable and the specified quiet-gap criterion is 5 ms, the third is separable from the earlier cluster. A pulse starting only 3 ms after the cluster ends would not be separately resolved by that rule even though it does not overlap. In analysing a series of reflections, update the cluster end to the latest end of any pulse that overlaps or lies within the specified quiet-gap threshold.

Absorbent wall treatments can reduce reflected amplitudes and late energy, usually reducing reverberation. They do not necessarily change path travel times significantly when geometry and medium stay fixed. A weak reflection can be physically present but absent from the detector's record. Moving the source, changing a wall, or changing pulse duration can change overlap and perceived clarity without necessarily altering every path. Avoid using loud sounds in demonstrations; reason from recorded or hypothetical data.

For advanced tasks, compare two proposed room or detector models by predicting arrival intervals and thresholded observations, then use an independent change of duration or sensitivity to eliminate alternatives. Distinguish an observed unresolved cluster from a claim that there is only one path. The present inspectable Core2 bank has no exact reverberation question; these constructions are authored transfer.

progressive_examples.problem: Direct and reflected pulses start 15 ms apart; pulse duration 20 ms. Do intervals overlap?
Pulses start at 0, 10, 35 ms, duration 8 ms, quiet gap 5 ms required. Group the record.
progressive_examples.reasoning: First two separated by only 2 ms quiet gap: one unresolved group; third starts 17 ms after second ends, separate.

progressive_examples.problem: Two rooms have identical visible leading times 0 and 40 ms, but one may have a weak return at 20 ms below threshold. What test distinguishes them?
progressive_examples.reasoning: Lower a calibrated detection threshold with sufficiently short pulse and quiet-gap rule; an additional detected 20 ms return supports the weak-path model.
progressive_examples.independent_check: A missing return at original threshold is not evidence of absence.

misconception.wrong_model: Each separate reflected path is automatically a distinct audible echo; a missing peak proves no reflected path exists.
misconception.diagnostic: Could two 20 ms pulses starting 10 ms apart be resolved as separate echoes? Could a weak path fall below threshold?
misconception.repair: Build arrival intervals and apply explicit resolution and amplitude conditions before interpreting the record.

exit_check.task: Three detectable pulses start 0, 7 and 30 ms, each 10 ms long; required quiet gap is 4 ms. How many resolved groups?
exit_check.reasoning: First two overlap; third has 13 ms gap.

core1b.fresh_task: Two detectable returns arrive 12 and 38 ms after direct sound. A brief click gives separated returns; a much longer source pulse gives blended sound. Explain why changed sound duration can alter echo perception without moving walls.
core1b.protected_work: Explain changing echo/reverberation observations through finite pulse overlap, reflection strength and detector limits, not a single distance rule.

stages.predict: Predict whether changing the source pulse duration can change perceived echo clarity without changing reflected travel times.
stages.attempt: Two detectable returns arrive 12 and 38 ms after direct sound. A brief click gives separated returns; a much longer source pulse gives blended sound. Explain why changed sound duration can alter echo perception without moving walls.
stages.reconstruct: Fixed path delays; longer pulses overlap or leave too small a quiet gap, producing blended persistence. Separability also depends on threshold and strength.
stages.diagnose: Identify whether you treated echo timing alone as a complete description of clarity or assumed a missing signal means no path.
stages.repair: Compare physical path delays, pulse intervals, amplitude and detection conditions; explain which changed and which did not.
stages.boundary_test: If the longer pulse is replaced by a short one but reflections are too weak, must separate echoes be heard?

Detector retains amplitudes ≥threshold and separates clusters only after quiet gap ≥4 ms. With duration 14 ms and threshold0.3, observed groups are 0–23 and 38–52 ms. Next change duration to 3 ms at threshold0.3, then threshold to0.1 at same duration; the last trace shows starts 0,9,21,38 ms. Test both models through all trials and explain what each intervention establishes.

stages.reconstruct: Initially both detect0,9,38 and group0–23,38–52. Short duration at old threshold separates0,9,38 (gaps6,26); both still fit. Lower threshold exposes21 only in B; all gaps≥4 after 3 ms. B fits three traces; duration resolves existing overlap, threshold exposes weak path. Not proof no further subthreshold paths.
